title: Calprotectin
desc: Calprotectin is an abundant neutrophil protein complex (an S100A8/S100A9 heterodimer) that helps defend the host by sequestering manganese and zinc from microbes, and is measured in stool as a biomarker of gut inflammation.

title: Dissimilatory Metal Reduction
desc: Dissimilatory metal reduction is a form of anaerobic microbial respiration in which cells conserve energy by transferring respiratory electrons onto an oxidized metal, such as Fe(III), Mn(IV), or U(VI), used as the terminal electron acceptor.

title: Irving–Williams Series
desc: The Irving–Williams series is the empirical order of thermodynamic stability for high-spin divalent first-row transition-metal complexes, Mn(II) < Fe(II) < Co(II) < Ni(II) < Cu(II) > Zn(II), which holds regardless of the ligand.

title: Metal Intoxication
desc: Metal intoxication is the offensive arm of nutritional immunity in which host immune cells flood a trapped microbe with toxic excess copper and zinc to mismetalate its enzymes and destroy iron-sulfur clusters.

title: Metal Sparing
desc: Metal sparing is the remodeling of a microbe's proteome during metal starvation, in which metal-requiring proteins are replaced by isozymes that use a different metal or no metal at all, thereby reducing cellular demand for the scarce element.

title: Metallochaperone
desc: A metallochaperone is a soluble intracellular carrier protein that binds a specific metal ion and delivers it by direct protein-protein contact to a designated target enzyme or transporter.

title: Metallome
desc: The metallome is the entirety of metal and metalloid species within a cell or organism, comprising free ions together with all metal- and metalloid-containing biomolecules.

title: Metallomics
desc: Metallomics is the integrated study of the metallome — the identity, quantity, distribution, coordination chemistry and biological function of all metals and metalloids in a cell, tissue or organism.

title: Metallophore
desc: A metallophore is a low-molecular-weight molecule secreted by microorganisms to bind and acquire a specific scarce metal ion from the environment or host.

title: Metalloproteome
desc: The metalloproteome is the complete set of metal-binding proteins in an organism or cell, encompassing every protein that requires a metal ion or metal cofactor for its structure or function.

title: Metalloregulation
desc: Metalloregulation is the process by which cells sense intracellular metal-ion concentrations through metal-responsive regulatory proteins that switch target genes on or off to maintain metal homeostasis.

title: Metallostasis
desc: Metallostasis is the coordinated sensing, buffering, trafficking, and sparing of metal ions that keeps each essential metal's bioavailability within a narrow physiological range inside a cell.

title: Mismetallation
desc: Mismetallation is the binding of a metalloprotein's metal site by the wrong metal ion — usually a more competitive one — which inactivates or misdirects the enzyme.

title: Nutritional Immunity
desc: Nutritional immunity is the host defense strategy of controlling transition-metal availability—withholding iron, zinc, and manganese or intoxicating microbes with copper and zinc—to limit the growth of invading pathogens.

title: Siderophore
desc: A siderophore is a small, high-affinity iron(III)-chelating molecule that microbes secrete to scavenge scarce environmental iron and import it into the cell.

title: Enough metal. Available to whom?
desc: Enough metal. Available to whom? Start here · An organizing thesis The most useful question in microbial metallomics is not simply how much metal is present. It is which organism can reach which chemical form, in which compartment, with what effect on host and community. This is the field guide’s editorial framework: connect chemistry, microbial function, host regulation, and clinical outcomes, with each connection labeled by the evidence supporting it. An organizing thesis for microbial metallomics: chemical form, compartments, host–microbial competition, zinc and MS, iron restriction, and testable evidence gaps. Metal amount is not metal access A supplement label describes an input. A blood result samples a circulating pool. A microbiome report describes a community through the assay used to measure it. None, alone, tells us where the metal went, who used it, or whether that use helped the host. The central task is to connect these observations rather than substitute one for another. Iron makes the distinction concrete: hepcidin can reduce ferroportin-mediated export from cells, restricting delivery to the circulation. Zinc offers a different example: an inflammatory metal-binding protein can disadvantage susceptible microbes while a competitor with effective acquisition machinery retains an advantage. “Less available” always needs an answer to “available to whom?” Five questions to ask of every metal–microbe claim Question What must be specified A misleading shortcut Chemical form Ion, oxidation state, ligand, particle, or metal-containing molecule; dissolution and transformation. Treating every compound containing the same element as the same exposure. Local pool Gut lumen, mucosa, blood, tissue, or an intracellular compartment; bound versus exchangeable metal. Calling a low blood value a map of the entire body. Access machinery Transporters, binding molecules, efflux, host sequestration, and their activity in that setting. Assuming a detected gene is active or every strain has the same capacity. Biological function What changes: enzyme activity, respiration, competition, barrier function, or immune behavior? Treating a taxonomic shift as the mechanism itself. Host outcome Absorption, cellular use, inflammation, symptoms, and disease course are distinct endpoints. Calling any microbiome change harmful, or any absorption increase therapeutic. These are linked questions, not a validated equation or risk score. The proposed advance of this atlas is to keep the connections visible—and to mark the ones the evidence has not yet made. Nutritional immunity has a geography Host defense does not always mean removing a metal. In a macrophage model, ATP7A-dependent copper trafficking contributed to bacterial killing. In separate work, the bacterial ligand yersiniabactin buffered copper toxicity, and copper–yersiniabactin complexes were detected in human urinary infection samples. Metal delivery and microbial protection can therefore oppose one another. These studies do not constitute a single experiment tracing the same copper pool. Location can also change the result of the same dietary intervention. In mice, a manganese-rich diet worsened staphylococcal infection in the heart without the same pattern in liver and kidney. Subsequent work implicated altered neutrophil function as well. A story about feeding a bacterium can miss an effect on the cell trying to contain it. This is why “high” and “low” require a specimen, compartment, method, and comparison. Hypozincemia means low circulating zinc; it does not name zinc status inside every immune cell. A tissue elemental map is not a measurement of its labile, readily exchangeable intracellular pool. The spatial question belongs beside the concentration. Zinc: better absorption is only one connection Formulation matters, but the comparison matters just as much. A preliminary crossover study in eight healthy adults estimated greater zinc absorption from aspartate than from gluconate or sulfate when given with milk. It did not test oxide. A different 15-person trial found lower absorption from oxide than from citrate or gluconate under its own conditions. Combining their percentages into an aspartate-versus-oxide ranking would combine different experiments. Supported in a small human study Aspartate can change estimated host absorption. The absorption finding is real within the tested protocol. It is an endpoint about the host. Direct measurement of the zinc remaining in the gut, its chemical availability, and microbial acquisition before claiming that aspartate bypasses microbes. Preclinical signal · human mechanism unresolved Aspartate has a preclinical signal in an MS model. Oral zinc aspartate improved experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis in mice. A small human MS trial studied sulfate and depression; it found no between-group difference in the neurological examinations reported. A human formulation comparison with disease outcomes and evidence that a microbial zinc mechanism mediates any benefit. Calprotectin fits the question but does not answer it by itself. Its abundance is not a measurement of zinc occupancy, zinc flux, or which organism acquired the withheld metal. Likewise, an MS-associated microbial community does not reveal its zinc economy simply from the species names. Human cohort associations and experimental immune effects provide reasons to investigate, not proof of zinc theft. Read the zinc comparison, compartment map, and MS evidence ledger Iron: depleted stores and restricted delivery are different problems Absolute iron deficiency means stores are depleted. In inflammatory iron restriction, iron may be retained in storage and recycling cells while its delivery for red-cell production is constrained. Both can coexist. These are two mechanisms to distinguish, not an exhaustive classification of anemia. Human inflammatory signaling experiments and cellular ferroportin experiments explain a route from inflammation to reduced circulating iron. The attractive hypothesis is that oral iron can increase intestinal microbial exposure while host delivery remains limited. That is a question about competing destinations, not proof that every unsuccessful course of ferrous sulfate fed a pathogen. In an IBD trial, oral and intravenous treatment produced different microbial and metabolic changes, while both improved iron deficiency; changes in disease activity were not dependent on route. Counterevidence must be visible. A South African child trial improved iron status without detecting changes in the measured bacterial groups, short-chain fatty acids, or fecal calprotectin. Its setting and targeted assays matter. The defensible claim is that microbial effects vary with the population, formulation, background ecology, and endpoint—not that replacement is intrinsically harmful. Read the iron map: depletion, restriction, delivery, and formulation A disease signature must become a functional question A list of taxa is the beginning of a hypothesis, not the end of a mechanism. A higher relative abundance can reflect a fall in another population. Species labels do not establish transporter content, expression, access to substrate, or actual metal transfer. Quantitative microbiome profiling in MS shows why bacterial load and confounding can change which associations remain robust. Chemical selectivity can be very specific: gut bacterial transporters distinguish vitamin B12-related corrinoids. These are cobalt-containing molecules, not interchangeable supplies of free cobalt. Transporter mobility can also change competitive behavior within a gut microbial species. Functional capacity cannot safely be frozen into a permanent “good” or “bad” species label. The missing links between a signature and an intervention Evidence layer What it contributes What remains unproved Community association A reproducible association after diet, medication, stool characteristics, and absolute load are considered. That the organisms cause the disease or share one metal-handling phenotype. Functional potential Genes and pathways that could acquire, transform, exclude, or redistribute a metal. That they are expressed, chemically supplied, or important in this host. Activity and flux Evidence of expression, metabolites, local chemical pools, and movement between compartments. That changing this flux changes the clinical outcome. Causal and clinical effect An intervention changes the proposed pathway and a meaningful host endpoint. Whether that pathway mediates the host effect; generalization beyond the tested population, formulation, and setting. The next useful “signature” would join microbial functions to host regulation and metal chemistry in the same people over time. That is a research objective. This site does not currently possess a validated signature that selects a supplement for an individual. Make the thesis capable of being wrong A strong mechanism is not automatically a successful treatment rule. Hepcidin predicted use of oral iron in children, yet a later hepcidin-guided strategy that reduced iron exposure was less effective at improving hemoglobin and failed its prespecified non-inferiority test. Prediction and intervention answer different questions. Test access, not just abundance The zinc and iron literature suggests a shared measurement problem: host uptake, microbial exposure, and clinical benefit are usually studied separately. A useful clinical research comparison would connect them prospectively. Define the actual formulation, food context, route, and relevant host state before comparing outcomes. Measure host uptake or use alongside a defensible estimate of the local available metal pool; total stool concentration alone is insufficient. Track microbial functions and absolute community measures, with inflammation, medications, and baseline deficiency considered. Specify the host endpoint and the result that would contradict the proposed microbial mechanism before interpreting the data. If a formulation improves host uptake without changing the proposed microbial pathway, its benefit may be real while the microbial-bypass explanation is wrong. A change in the microbiome is also not a clinical endpoint by itself. In one mouse study, oral vitamin B12 changed distal-gut corrinoids and selected bacterial abundances without improving or worsening the measured colitis outcome. Null and discordant results help identify which part of a story actually explains the host. Use the atlas as a map of connections Read each profile in two directions: from the chemical form toward the host outcome, and backward from a disease observation toward the measurements needed to explain it. Zinc and iron are the first full worked examples of this approach. Across the broader atlas, distinguish a demonstrated mechanism from a plausible connection and a proposed test. title: Karen Pendergrass
desc: Karen Pendergrass investigates upstream metal contamination in food systems and agricultural inputs, and how these exposures may influence microbial metabolism and disease. Her work connects exposure pathways with mismetallation and metal-dependent enzyme function, with particular attention to nickel, urease, [NiFe]-hydrogenases, and nickel-dependent forms of glyoxalase I. By examining microbiome and metallomic signatures together, she explores how changes in metal availability and enzyme activity may link microbial communities and heavy-metal exposure to conditions such as endometriosis and Parkinson’s disease. She is the founder of Microbiome Medicine, Heavy Metal Index, Wikibiome, and the Institute of Contaminant Standards (ICS).

title: Iron & microbes
desc: Fe Iron stores, inflammatory restriction, microbial access, and formulation-dependent outcomes Iron is a nutrient, an enzyme cofactor, and an environmental electron acceptor. In the host, depleted stores and restricted delivery are distinct problems that may coexist. A useful microbial account must follow iron into local chemical pools, then connect acquisition and competition to host benefit or harm. Iron deficiency Hepcidin Siderophores Human intervention Environmental redox Kenyan infants receiving micronutrient powders Two mechanisms of iron shortage—and their overlap Anemia describes a red-cell or hemoglobin problem; it is not itself a diagnosis of iron depletion. Absolute deficiency and inflammatory restriction are two important iron mechanisms, not the only causes of anemia. Their overlap matters: a person can have inflammation and genuinely depleted stores. Distinguish the pool from the delivery problem State Mechanistic picture Interpretive limit Absolute depletion Stores are reduced, limiting iron available for erythropoiesis. Inflammation can coexist; a single circulating result does not resolve the mixture. Inflammatory restriction IL-6 can increase hepcidin; hepcidin reduces ferroportin-mediated cellular export, limiting circulating delivery. This is regulated iron redistribution, not evidence that all iron in all tissues is excessive. Mixed deficiency and inflammation In an IBD cohort, low ferritin accompanied low hepcidin despite inflammatory activity. Inflammation does not automatically establish high hepcidin in every patient. The phrase “the body is trying to get iron out of the labile pool” needs a specified pool. Hepcidin–ferroportin biology concerns export and systemic availability; it is not a direct measurement of labile iron inside every cell. In a small marrow-characterized rheumatoid arthritis cohort, additional iron markers helped distinguish deficient stores and predict response—illustrating why the diagnostic question needs more than anemia alone. Depletion & restriction Oral iron: separate host response from microbial effects Randomized human route comparison Microbial change did not equal clinical worsening. In a trial including Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, and noninflamed iron-deficient controls, oral sulfate and intravenous sucrose produced distinct microbial and metabolic changes. Both improved iron deficiency; disease-activity changes were independent of route. A demonstrated causal chain from a particular iron-access function to a clinically important outcome. Randomized human counterexample Ferrous sulfate did not disrupt every measured community. In iron-deficient South African schoolchildren, supplementation improved iron status without detected changes in ten measured bacterial groups, fecal short-chain fatty acids, or calprotectin. Broader functional measurements and replication in other ecologies; a targeted null result is not proof of no possible effect. These findings sit beside the Kenyan infant fortification studies above. Different baseline ecology, age, formulation, and measurement scope can produce different results. It is plausible that unabsorbed iron supports some organisms, but identifying that path requires more than a poor hemoglobin response or an increase in relative abundance. Host feedback also changes exposure over time. Stable-isotope studies in iron-depleted women found that oral sulfate increased hepcidin and reduced absorption of a subsequent dose. The fraction absorbed and the absolute amount absorbed are different quantities. Timing is part of the mechanism; this experiment does not provide a microbiome-based dosing rule. Host & microbial outcomes A formulation can matter without proving microbial exclusion The IHAT-GUT phase II trial randomized 642 young Gambian children to iron hydroxide adipate tartrate, ferrous sulfate, or placebo. IHAT met the trial’s non-inferiority criterion for the composite efficacy endpoint. The rate of moderate-to-severe diarrhea was lower than with sulfate, while the proportion experiencing at least one such episode was similar. These are different safety measures. Interpret the comparison at its actual scale: phase II, different elemental doses selected for estimated comparable bioavailability, and 80% confidence intervals. The result supports further formulation research; it does not prove general superiority or establish that a particular pathogen was denied iron. Formulation evidence The decisive question is where replacement goes Measure host use and microbial exposure together A stronger study would distinguish failure to absorb, restricted export, inadequate stores, ongoing losses, and microbial competition instead of assigning every weak response to the microbiome. Characterize iron stores and inflammatory context, accounting for mixed states. Measure host incorporation or a meaningful hematologic response alongside the local iron species accessible to microbes. Connect microbial acquisition functions and metabolites to absolute community changes, rather than treat a taxonomic list as a flux measurement. Judge the formulation using host efficacy and clinical adverse outcomes as well as microbial endpoints. If host response improves with no change in the proposed microbial function, that function is not established as the mediator. A final caution against overconfident precision: hepcidin predicted oral iron utilization in one study, but a later hepcidin-guided child trial reduced iron exposure at the cost of a worse hemoglobin response and failed non-inferiority. Mechanistic plausibility must survive a clinical comparison. Discriminating the mechanisms

title: Zinc & microbes
desc: Zn Chemical form, host–microbial access, and the missing links in zinc–MS hypotheses Zinc connects nutrient acquisition, host metal withholding, and competition with other metals. Its effects depend on the accessible pool and the organisms sharing it. Human absorption comparisons, microbial models, and MS research answer different parts of that question; the sections below keep their connections and missing links visible. Zinc formulations Nutritional immunity Calprotectin Multiple sclerosis Compartmental zinc Inflamed mouse intestine Mouse C. difficile infection A zinc result needs a compartment Measurements that answer different questions Pool or signal What the evidence measures What it cannot identify alone Blood One MS cohort had lower average serum zinc than controls, generally within reference ranges; treatment was a relevant covariate. Whole-body depletion, intestinal microbial capture, or zinc inside a specific immune-cell population. Chronic MS lesions Elemental imaging found lower zinc in chronic white-matter lesions than in surrounding normal-appearing white matter, accompanying myelin loss. A labile intracellular pool; the iron-rich lesion-rim pattern should not be reassigned to zinc. Immune cells A ZIP3 study linked cytosolic zinc regulation to pathogenic Th17-cell function in EAE. That a human dietary zinc form caused the cellular state or would correct it. Calprotectin An inflammatory protein with metal-withholding activity. Zinc-binding occupancy, microbial zinc uptake, or the source of a patient’s low circulating zinc. Use “hypozincemia” for low circulating zinc. Describe low or excess tissue zinc with its anatomical and chemical context. Lower serum zinc and a zinc-dependent pathogenic cell process are not logically inconsistent; they concern different pools. Zinc compartments Formulation evidence: compare like with like What the zinc studies actually compared Study and setting Observed result Boundary of inference Aspartate / gluconate / sulfate · 8 healthy adults Greater estimated fractional absorption with aspartate in a crossover study with milk. Preliminary, indirect urinary isotope estimate; no oxide, microbes, or MS arm. Citrate / gluconate / oxide · 15 healthy adults, without food Oxide absorption was lower; a few participants absorbed little or none. Different conditions and isotope method; no aspartate arm. Oxide / aspartate and other forms · digestion and Caco-2 model Oxide was somewhat less available in the tested intestinal model. An in vitro comparison is not a human head-to-head trial. Higher host absorption does not establish intact-chelate transport, bacterial exclusion, or preferential delivery to the cells that need zinc. Less unabsorbed mass might alter microbial exposure, but the chemical availability and site of that residual zinc remain separate questions. The human studies above cannot prove that aspartate goes straight to the host while oxide feeds its microbiota. Compare formulations MS: separate the evidence before connecting it Animal intervention Aspartate has a genuine preclinical signal. Oral zinc aspartate reduced clinical and histopathological EAE signs. Human MS efficacy, a direct oxide comparator, and microbial mediation. Small human trial · symptom outcome The clinical zinc study tested sulfate. In 43 people with MS and depression, a 12-week sulfate trial improved depression scores; reported neurological examinations did not differ between groups. An aspartate trial and adequately tested disease-course outcomes. Human association · functional potential A microbial pathway can suggest a mineral question. The household-paired iMSMS study found increased phytate-degradation pathway potential in untreated MS. This suggests a question about mineral release, not measured zinc transfer. Pathway activity, zinc speciation and flux, and who acquires any released mineral. Quantitative cohort · confounding matters MS-associated taxa do not establish zinc handling. A quantitative MS study showed that bacterial load and covariates materially affect associations, including the robustness of Akkermansia findings. A reproducible microbial-function signature that predicts formulation response. The assembled evidence does not establish that ordinary zinc oxide supplementation worsens MS, or that aspartate helps human MS by denying zinc to microbes. Those are hypotheses with several missing connections, not interchangeable summaries of these studies. MS evidence ledger What would discriminate the explanations? Pair host absorption with microbial access A useful formulation comparison would test whether the putative advantage is improved host uptake, changed local microbial access, an immune effect, or some combination. The existing absorption and EAE studies do not distinguish these explanations. Use a direct comparison in the same population and food context, with matched interpretation of elemental input and host uptake. Characterize residual intestinal zinc chemistry alongside microbial acquisition functions; species abundance alone is insufficient. Keep calprotectin, circulating zinc, microbial function, and clinical outcomes as separate measurements. For MS, account for disease-modifying treatment and assess a prespecified clinical endpoint rather than infer benefit from a microbiome shift. If host uptake improves but microbial access does not change, reject the bypass explanation without discarding the absorption result. Discriminating the mechanisms

title: Scandium & microbes
desc: Sc Modulation of bacterial gene expression Scandium can alter bacterial gene expression and the production of extracellular enzymes and secondary metabolites. It is a rare-earth element, but not a lanthanide. The evidence here concerns a culture condition that changes microbial behavior, rather than an established scandium-containing enzyme or a universal nutritional requirement. Rare earth Secondary metabolism Gene expression Bacterial culture Streptomyces coelicolor A3(2)

title: Rubidium & microbes
desc: Rb Transport through potassium-handling systems Rubidium is useful for understanding how bacteria distinguish chemically similar alkali-metal ions. It can enter through potassium-handling systems and can partly substitute for potassium under some culture conditions. Transportability, however, is not the same as physiological equivalence: the transporter, strain, and potassium background change the result. Alkali metal Potassium transport Ion selectivity Bacterial culture E. coli potassium transport systems

title: Americium & microbes
desc: Am Microbial accumulation and biosorption Americium research in microbes is mainly about binding and partitioning rather than a demonstrated biological redox cycle. Bacteria, fungal biomass, and dissolved microbial products can change how americium distributes between water, cells, and mineral surfaces. title: Yttrium & microbes
desc: Y Binding to microbial biomass Yttrium has direct microbial evidence for biosorption and for recognition by a selective metal-binding protein. Neither observation establishes that bacteria require yttrium for growth. Although grouped with the rare-earth elements, yttrium is not a lanthanide, and its biology should be evaluated on its own evidence. title: Follow the metal.
desc: Follow the metal. A qualitative mechanism explorer Choose a case. Trace the compartments. Find the connection that still needs evidence. These diagrams organize findings from distinct studies. Arrows describe a proposed route through the question; they do not mean that every step has been demonstrated in one experiment. There are no calculated doses or predicted patient outcomes. Explore zinc absorption, iron restriction, copper defense, and corrinoid selection through sourced compartment diagrams and explicit missing evidence. Zinc · absorption and competition Human absorption + separate microbial models Does more zinc reach the host—or less reach the microbes? One input, two access questions Formulation in the gut Aspartate, oxide, sulfate, and gluconate are formulation labels. The human comparisons tested different subsets under different food and measurement conditions. Host branch · uptake A higher absorbed fraction describes entry into the host. It does not identify how much remaining zinc is usable by a particular gut organism. Microbial branch · local access Calprotectin and microbial acquisition machinery can change competition in an inflamed niche. This was studied separately from the human formulation comparisons. The tempting inference is that better host absorption leaves less zinc for microbes. That may change total residual exposure, but chemical accessibility, timing, and location still need measurement. “Aspartate bypasses microbes” remains an untested explanation in the evidence assembled here. Open the formulation and MS evidence ledger Iron · stores and delivery Cellular mechanism + human intervention evidence The dose enters the gut. Does usable iron reach the marrow? Separate entry, export, and use Intestinal exposure Oral replacement introduces iron into the lumen. Its microbial and metabolic effects can differ from intravenous delivery. Host export Hepcidin binding to ferroportin reduces cellular iron export. Iron can be retained while circulating delivery falls. Red-cell production Hemoglobin response is a host outcome, not a direct readout of microbial feeding. A biomarker-guided reduction in exposure did not preserve efficacy in one child trial. First distinguish depleted stores, inflammatory restriction, and mixtures. Even in inflammatory bowel disease, depleted stores can accompany low hepcidin. Inflammation does not guarantee a closed export gate in every patient. Open the iron depletion and restriction map Copper · delivery and buffering Distinct cellular, chemical, and human-specimen studies A metal delivered as a defense can meet a microbial buffer. Opposing processes, assembled across studies Host trafficking A macrophage study implicated ATP7A-dependent copper delivery in antibacterial activity. Microbial ligand Yersiniabactin binds copper and can protect bacteria from its toxicity. Infection compartment Copper–yersiniabactin complexes were detected in human urinary infection specimens. Detection does not establish their contribution to each patient’s severity. The missing connection is simultaneous measurement of host delivery, ligand-bound versus accessible copper, and the host outcome in the same setting. A total copper result cannot supply all three. These studies do not establish that changing dietary copper would reproduce either mechanism. Read the copper profile Cobalt · molecule and transporter Gut bacterial mechanisms + a mouse supplementation study The cobalt atom does not tell you who can use the molecule. Chemical identity meets selective access Corrinoid mixture Vitamin B12 and related corrinoids contain cobalt. Their molecular differences matter to microbial use. Transporter repertoire Multiple transporters can discriminate among analogs; transferable transport capacity can change competition within a species. Community and host Oral B12 altered distal-gut corrinoids and some bacterial abundances in mice without changing the measured colitis outcome. The transporter studies have not shown that transporter selectivity caused the separate supplementation-associated community shift. Nor do they establish whether a particular community’s corrinoid handling limits host benefit in a defined clinical setting. Free cobalt supplementation is not an equivalent intervention.
